american-cycle: rules reference

Generated from the engine (config {{CONFIG_NAME}}, build {{BUILD_FINGERPRINT}}) by node docs/build.ts. Never edit docs/rules.html by hand — edit docs/rules.template.html or the engine, then regenerate. If a number here is wrong, the engine is wrong, not the prose.

A player is a faction, not a party: your hand holds cards of both D and R, and you choose which races to enter and which party to run each candidate under. Fifty states' worth of races come up on a fixed cycle; you can only afford to contest a fraction of them, so the game is about choosing which fraction.

The turn

Each year: draft a pack of candidate and district cards, declare candidates into open races, a window to withdraw before the dice are visible, elections resolve, the legislature votes on the year's omnibill, and lean decays toward zero everywhere. Your hand holds {{HAND_SIZE}} cards at the start of a cycle under {{CONFIG_NAME}} — far fewer than the races on the board, which is why most of them go uncontested.

How a race resolves

Every race rolls three six-sided dice per side: national (shared by every race your party runs that year — a wave), state (shared by every race your party runs in that state), and candidate (yours alone). Add a flat modifier total from your cards, highest sum wins.

A general election rolls the candidate die once per side. A primary shares its national and state die between both sides (same party, same state), so only the candidate die differs between them — and it rolls twice, not once, so no modifier gap is a certain thing.

A primary is decided by a much narrower die than a general, which is why a small identity-tag or incumbency edge matters far more in a primary than a general — and why a wide edge in a primary is close to a lock, while the same edge in a general still leaves real room for an upset.

Lean: the map's memory

Every state carries a signed lean, deviation from that state's own baseline (not from a national 50/50 — exactly like Cook PVI). Winning a race pushes the state's lean toward your party; how far depends on how decisively you won it:

{{PUSH_TABLE}}

Lean decays one pip per state per year, toward zero, so a state only realigns under a sustained run of results, not a single blowout. A newly elected president also places a one-pip honeymoon counter in every state they carried, gone by the next decay.

The most nationalized race on the ballot is the one that pushes lean, in this order: {{OFFICE_PRIORITY}}. A governor's race never pushes on its own — it only ever rides along when it agrees with the state's existing lean, which is why governors of the "wrong" party for their state (a Baker, a Hogan) are common and unremarkable.

Identity and demographics

Candidates and districts both carry tags from the same vocabulary, so a candidate's fit with a district — or a bill's fit with a bloc — is just overlap in the same space: {{TAG_LIST}}.

The legislature

One omnibill a year: it needs a House majority and {{SENATE_PASSAGE}} of the Senate to pass, can be vetoed and overridden at {{VETO_OVERRIDE}}, and an impeachment vote needs {{IMPEACH_THRESHOLD}}. Passage is scored by yes-vote, doubled for the majority party — so a bill is worth authoring even when you cannot claim it outright.

Scoring

Nothing accumulates. At the end of each year your score is read off what you still hold:

{{SCORING_TABLE}}

Anything repealed, reversed or unseated scores zero from then on — a score can fall without any decay rule at all.

The amendment

The one earned ending, proposed either of two ways. On config {{CONFIG_NAME}}, the ordinary route is Congress: {{AMENDMENT_CONGRESS}} of the House and {{AMENDMENT_CONGRESS}} of the Senate, with no presentment to the president — Article V gives the president no role in proposing an amendment. The rare route is a state convention: {{AMENDMENT_CALL}} states to call one. Either way, ratification needs {{AMENDMENT_RATIFY}} states, and {{AMENDMENT_BLOCK}} states block it outright — so a narrow leader can never close the game alone, and a determined minority always has a wall. Ratification does not name a winner outright; it ends the game and the epilogue score (above) decides who won.
